text: Everything so far in this chapter has been about reading and measuring circuits someone else built. This lesson flips the direction: starting from a plain-English target state, you work forward to a verified circuit that produces it — the actual day-to-day skill of writing quantum programs.

The specification: take ket-00 to ket-00 minus ket-11, over root 2. That's almost the standard Bell state, except for one relative minus sign on the ket-11 term. A sign flip on exactly one term is exactly what a Z gate does, and since CNOT only fires when its control is 1, applying Z to qubit 1 right after the Hadamard, and before the CNOT, should carry that minus sign through and land it specifically on ket-11. That's the design intuition — now it has to be checked, not trusted.

Starting from ket-00: H on qubit 1 gives 0.7071, 0, 0.7071, 0. Z on qubit 1 flips the sign wherever qubit 1 reads 1, giving 0.7071, 0, negative 0.7071, 0. CNOT with qubit 1 as control then swaps the ket-10 and ket-11 amplitudes, landing on 0.7071, 0, 0, negative 0.7071 — exactly ket-00 minus ket-11 over root 2, confirmed term by term, not assumed from the pattern.

With the sequence verified, the circuit diagram is H and Z on qubit 1's wire, then a control dot tied down to an X on qubit 2's wire — H and Z both happen before anything touches qubit 2, and CNOT is the final, connecting operation. That's the complete answer: not just a state vector, but something you could hand to someone else to build.

Next lesson works through three more specifications with this exact same workflow — known recipe, identify the gap, verify numerically, then diagram — including one case where no entangling gate is needed at all.
